planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; John's is not self-fertile and should be planted alongside Adams, Nova, or another distinct elderberry cultivar for reliable pollination and a full crop.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; pair with a second, genetically distinct elderberry cultivar within cross-pollinating range for a full crop, since John's does not set well on its own. John's is one of the oldest named Canadian elderberry selections, long grown as a classic pollinator and companion cultivar for Adams in commercial and home elderberry plantings — the two cultivars were historically recommended together as a standard cross-pollinating pair for decades before more recent university releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood became available. The tall, vigorous shrub produces large, flat-topped flower clusters in early summer, valued for elderflower tea, cordial, and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer used for jams, syrups, wine, and traditional elderberry preparations. Its long track record and reliable vigor make it a solid, time-tested choice for a home elderberry planting, especially paired with Adams for cross-pollination, zone 3–8.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
University of Missouri Extension — Elderberry Production

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Anna is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine (such as 'Meader' or a seedling male) within about 30–50 feet for pollination and fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola, since mature vines become heavy and vigorous.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, with a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor structure in place before planting. Anna is one of the most widely planted female hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivars in North America, valued for its heavy, reliable production of smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit that can be eaten whole, skin and all, unlike fuzzy supermarket kiwifruit. The fruit ripens in early fall with sweet, richly flavored, bright green flesh, and the vigorous vine is notably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below what damages standard fuzzy kiwi (Actinidia deliciosa). As a dioecious cultivar, Anna requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine planted nearby for pollination — without one, the vine will grow and flower but set little to no fruit. A vigorous, productive choice for a well-supported arbor or fence line in zone 4–8.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Geneva is a female cultivar developed at Cornell's Geneva, New York research station and requires a male hardy kiwi vine within pollinating range for fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola for the vigorous vine.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a permanent, sturdy support structure. Geneva is a female hardy kiwi cultivar selected and released by Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural research station, bred for excellent fruit quality, good productivity, and reliable cold hardiness suited to northern growing conditions. The smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit ripens in fall with sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi, eaten whole without peeling, and the vine's Cornell breeding gives it dependable performance and disease tolerance in the humid Northeast, translating well to other regions with cold winters. As with all Actinidia arguta, Geneva is dioecious and needs a separate male vine planted nearby to ensure pollination and fruit set. A well-vetted, university-tested choice for a hardy kiwi arbor in zone 4–8.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Ken's Red is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine within pollinating range for fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola, since mature vines are vigorous and heavy once fruiting.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor. Ken's Red is a female hardy kiwi cultivar originating in New Zealand, distinguished from most other Actinidia arguta selections by its attractive reddish-purple fruit skin and red-blushed flesh near the skin, in addition to the sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi. The smooth skin means the small, grape-sized fruit can be eaten whole without peeling, and its distinctive red coloring makes it a visually striking choice for a home fruit planting or farmers-market crop. Like all Actinidia arguta, it is dioecious and needs a separate male vine nearby to ensure good pollination and a full fruit set. A flavorful, ornamental option for gardeners who want something visually distinct from standard green-fleshed hardy kiwi, zone 4–8.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
New Zealand Plant Variety Rights Office

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Meader is a male cultivar grown solely to pollinate female hardy kiwi vines (such as Anna, Geneva, or Ken's Red) — it produces no fruit itself. One male vine can pollinate several female vines within about 30–50 feet.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis; site centrally within pollinating distance of the female vines it is meant to serve. Meader is a male hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivar selected by Professor Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, prized specifically for its exceptional cold hardiness — among the most cold-tolerant hardy kiwi selections available, able to survive winter conditions that damage or kill less hardy male cultivars. As a male vine, it produces abundant flowers but no fruit; its sole purpose in the garden is to provide pollen for nearby female cultivars, and because Actinidia arguta is dioecious, at least one male vine is essential wherever female vines are grown for fruit. Its outstanding hardiness makes it the standard pollinator choice for northern hardy kiwi plantings, ensuring the pollinator survives winters that a female cultivar chosen for fruit quality alone might not, zone 3–8.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide
